title: Level 1: Single Abstractions (~10–12 years)

html:
The individual becomes capable of constructing single abstractions-general concepts that are built by identifying what is common across multiple representational systems. Fischer emphasizes that abstractions constitute a qualitatively different kind of cognitive structure, one that is extracted from concrete instances but no longer reducible to them.

What characterizes this level is that the abstraction functions like a new mental variable ("the same kind of thing is happening here") that can organize judgments and actions, but it’s usually still one-at-a-time: you can deploy one abstract dimension robustly without yet coordinating multiple abstractions into a larger structure.

Example 1: Variables and Arithmetic Operations

The child understands a "variable" as a thing they can operate on: understanding that xx stands for "any number" and using that idea across different problems, without needing a concrete number each time. The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

The child constructs "multiplication" as an abstract operation, a general procedure that applies to any two quantities, including quantities she has never encountered and quantities too large to visualize (e.g., 347x892). The abstraction captures the structure of the operation independent of any particular content (i.e axb=a+a+a+...+aaxb=a+a+a+...+a). These abstractions can now be applied to novel problems, manipulated symbolically, and reasoned about as entities in their own right ("multiplication makes numbers bigger... except when one number is less than one").

At the Representational level, the child might understand that 3x4=12 by thinking of it as "three groups of four objects," perhaps visualized as three rows of four apples. She can solve specific multiplication problems and may even recognize patterns across several problems. However, her understanding remains tied to these concrete instantiations-she is manipulating mental images of grouped objects.

Example 2: Moral Abstractions

The child starts using fairness as a general principle rather than a case-by-case preference: they can look at splitting candy, taking turns in a game, or sharing chores and say (and act as if) "it should be equal" or "it should match contribution," even when the surface details differ. The key is that "fairness" is no longer "what we did last time" or "what mom said," but an abstract property they can carry across situations.

The child extracts the abstraction honesty as a general property that people can possess and that characterizes a category of actions. Honesty becomes an intangible entity-it cannot be seen or touched, it is not identical to any single act of truth-telling, yet it is understood as something real that organizes and explains diverse behaviors. A younger child at the representational tier understands specific instances of honesty and dishonesty: "I told Mom I didn’t eat the cookie, but I did-that was lying" or "Sarah said she liked my drawing even though she didn’t." These are concrete representational systems tied to particular events, actors, and contexts.

At this level, however, the child holds their moral abstractions in isolation. They cannot yet systematically coordinate "honesty" with other moral abstractions like "kindness" or "loyalty". For instance, reasoning about what to do when being honest would hurt someone’s feelings (which requires coordinating "honesty" and "kindness").

Example 3: Personality Traits

Previously, a child might say "My friend gave me his lunch, and he helped me with homework, and he always waits for me." The child describes a system of behaviors. Now, the child might say "My friend is kind" or "He is generous."

The child extracts a single, abstract personality trait ("Kindness") that explains all the disparate concrete behaviors. "Kindness" isn’t an action you can see; it’s an invisible internal quality that causes the actions.

At this level, however, the abstraction is often rigid. A person is "Kind." If they do something mean, the 10-year-old is confused (similar to the Level 7 "dog vs. toy" confusion when seeing a toy dog). They cannot yet coordinate "Kindness" with "Stress".

Example 4: Theme Identification (Literature)

Previously, a child writes a book report summarizing the plot: "The boy went to the mountain, fought the dragon, and came back home." They track the complex sequence of events. Now, the student identifies the theme: "This story is about courage." The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

"Courage" is not an event in the book. It is an abstract concept that summarizes the emotional weight of the concrete events. The student has moved from "what happened" to "what it means.

Example 5: Energy

In elementary science, children learn concrete examples: a ball rolling down a ramp, a battery powering a light bulb, food giving you strength to run. These are representational systems-specific scenarios understood in terms of their particular objects and actions.

Now, the student constructs energy as a single abstraction: an invisible quantity that exists in different forms, can be transferred between objects, and explains why things happen. Energy is not any particular instance of "stuff that makes things go"-it is the general concept that unifies all such instances. The student can now:

Identify energy in novel situations ("the wind has energy")

Discuss energy without reference to any specific system

Understand that energy is conserved as a general principle
